name: Felix Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for joining me, Felix. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you say is confidential. You can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a patrol constable in Hillcrest, the northern suburbs, so it's burglaries, car thefts off driveways, kids on scooters, the odd missing teenager. Two days a month I train with the force's drone unit, which is the best part of my job by miles. I fly the practice drone over the old quarry and they show me how to search for someone with the heat camera.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you use AI tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Every day. I use one to quiz me on law, one to plan my study, and I ask it to explain drone flight rules when the manual is confusing. My sergeant says I'm quick to learn and quick to rush, which is fair. I got a written warning last year for bagging evidence in the wrong order on a burglary.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Sam in a rented terrace on Holly Road. Sam's a software tester at a bank, so between us we're fine month to month, but we've got an electric car on finance and almost nothing saved, maybe three weeks. We keep saying we'll start a savings pot and then the car insurance comes round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. Honestly, a bit of a letdown. I like the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was overhyped, but the useful bits are still useful, like drafting and translation. At the station I'd keep showing people the shortcuts I use. Online I'd probably post a few tips for other new officers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'm fine. My job's steady, Sam's job's steady, it's just money that's tight because of the car and the rent. The warning on my file worries me more than any computer, because it could slow down my drone unit application.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, stay on the drone training days and apply for the unit when the next post comes up. I'd set up an automatic savings transfer of a hundred a month, even if it hurts. And I'd go back over the evidence rules properly with a checklist, so I never get another warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit bored by the idea of nothing changing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the warning worries you more than computers. What happened that day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I was rushing to get to another call and bagged a crowbar before photographing where it was. The sergeant caught it, and it was fine in court in the end. But it's on my file, and the drone unit checks files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a hundred a month cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the gaming subscription and two takeaways a month. Sam would say we can do more. Sam's better with money than I am, which isn't hard.

say: AI was **overhyped**, but drafting and translation still help.
I'd post **tips for new officers** on the tools I use.
think: Our jobs are **steady**; money is tight because of the car and rent.
The **written warning** on my file worries me more than any computer.
do: Apply for the **drone unit** when the next post opens.
Set up a **hundred-a-month** automatic savings transfer.
Go over evidence rules with a **checklist** to avoid another warning.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit bored by nothing changing.
S0.quote: I was rushing to get to another call and bagged a crowbar before photographing where it was.
fieldNote: An **early adopter** who is honest about rushing and a mark on his file.
Household income feels secure in this case, but **no cushion** and car finance keep him uneasy.
His goal is the **drone unit**, the hands-on tech side of policing.

steps.text: Keep going to the drone training days at the quarry
Set up a hundred-a-month automatic savings transfer
Apply for the force drone unit when a post opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, this one's interesting, because it's two different stories in our house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say this is good for policing if they put the time saved into patrols. I'd volunteer to help roll out the new tools. Online I'd be one of the people saying don't panic, learn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm okay, but Sam isn't. Software testing is checking and coding, which is right at the top of the card. If the bank cuts testers, we lose more than half our income and we can't cover the car and the rent on my pay. So I'd be fine at work and worried at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard for the drone unit, because flying and searching is hands-on with a bit of tech, a good mix. I'd help Sam look at other work, maybe testing for medical devices where the rules are stricter. And we'd start cutting now: sell the electric car and get something cheap, so the finance stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a busy way. I'd be making lists, not lying awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Sam the night the bank announces cuts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a plan and we're not going to lose the house. Then I'd open the laptop and make a spreadsheet, because that's what I do. Sam would probably tell me to close it and just sit for a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd sell the car. What does that save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The finance is two hundred and eighty a month, and we owe about nine thousand. If we sold it and bought an old hatchback for three, we'd clear most of it. It feels like going backwards, but it's the smart move.

say: AI is good if the **time saved** goes into patrols.
I'd tell people online **don't panic, learn it**.
think: I'm okay, but Sam's **software testing** job is at the top of the card.
Without Sam's pay, we **can't cover** the car and the rent.
do: Push hard for the **drone unit**, a mix of tech and hands-on.
Help Sam look at **medical device testing**, where rules are stricter.
Sell the **electric car** and buy a cheap hatchback to end the finance.
feel: **Anxious** in a busy way, making lists rather than lying awake.
S1.quote: I'd be fine at work and worried at home.
fieldNote: The risk here is **his partner's income**, not his own job.
Adaptive and practical: he'd **sell the car** quickly to cut finance costs.
Sees the **drone unit** as a good mix of tech and hands-on work.

steps.text: Volunteer to help roll out the new AI tools at the station
Apply for the drone unit's next open post
Sell the electric car and buy an old hatchback
Help Sam apply for medical device testing jobs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the fast ones. This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That changes everything at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a national plan, fast: income support for people whose jobs go, retraining that's actually funded. At work I'd say it's coming, so let's be the officers who understand it. Online I'd probably be more serious than usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, Sam's job is gone by 2028, I'm almost sure. My reports, statements and planning go too, so the force wants fewer officers, and the drone unit gets automated drones. The bit that lasts is the hands-on stuff, which robots take around 2031. I'd have maybe three years, and the household would be on one low wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take every course the force offers on the new systems, so I'm the one they keep to supervise them. I'd sell the car within a month and cut everything else. And I'd ask the force about the drone unit straight away, because someone has to oversee the automated drones, at least for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, honestly. I like change, but not change that takes the floor away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap mean for you specifically?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the difference between being useful and being gone. From 2028 to 2031 the force still needs people who can go to a door and handle things. If I'm the officer who can also run the AI and the drones, I'm in the last group they let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you and Sam move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in with Sam's parents, who have a spare room in the next town. It would be hard, and my commute would be an hour. But with one wage and no savings, rent on Holly Road is the first thing that has to go.

say: We need a **national plan**: income support and funded retraining.
Officers should be **the ones who understand** the new systems.
think: **Sam's job** is almost surely gone by 2028.
Fewer officers will be needed, and our household would be on **one low wage**.
do: Take every force course on **new systems** to be the one supervising them.
Sell the **car within a month** and cut all extras.
Ask about **overseeing automated drones** in the drone unit.
feel: **Scared**, because this change takes the floor away.
S2.quote: If I'm the officer who can also run the AI and the drones, I'm in the last group they let go.
fieldNote: The fast case puts **both incomes** at risk; one goes almost at once.
He uses the **three-year gap** as a ladder: be the one who supervises machines.
Even an adaptive person is **alarmed** with no savings and a partner out of work.

steps.text: Take every force course on the new AI systems
Sell the electric car within a month
Move into Sam's parents' spare room in the next town
Campaign for funded retraining and income support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Same end point, more time. This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2031. Five years. Okay, that's a real window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got time to do it right, so the force should plan who moves where. I'd want to help design how the tools are used. Online I'd share how-to guides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years lets Sam switch to something safer and lets me get into the drone unit and become the tech person there. It's still tight, because when AGI hits in 2031 the paperwork side of everything goes. But I'd be thirty-two with skills that matter until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd get the drone pilot qualification the force pays for, and apply to the unit. I'd sell the car, put the savings in a separate account, and aim for three months of cushion by 2029. And I'd encourage Sam to start an evening course in something hands-on, maybe electrical installs for solar panels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in control. I'd be busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Sam could do electrical work. Has Sam ever done anything like that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sam built half our shed and rewired the lamp in the hallway, so a bit. Sam likes fixing things more than testing software, honestly. Five years is enough to retrain if we start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would three months of cushion look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About five thousand. We'd get there by 2029 if the car's gone and we put three hundred a month aside. It's the first time I'd ever have that much in the bank.

say: We have time, so the force should **plan who moves** where.
I'd want to help **design how tools** are used.
think: Five years lets Sam **switch** and lets me join the drone unit.
My skills would matter until about **2034**, when robots arrive.
do: Get the **drone pilot qualification** this year and apply to the unit.
Sell the car and aim for **five thousand** saved by 2029.
Encourage Sam to start an **evening electrical** course.
S3.quote: Five years is enough to retrain if we start now.
fieldNote: Five years turns panic into a **household plan** for both partners.
He would have **real savings** for the first time.
Still anxious because **Sam's job change** isn't certain.

steps.text: Get the force-funded drone pilot qualification this year
Save three hundred a month toward five thousand by 2029
Help Sam enrol in an evening solar electrical course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the slowest. This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036. Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's plenty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best case: enough time to retrain people properly. At work I'd be the guy saying let's start small and learn the tools now. Online I'd keep sharing guides.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years feels good for me. I'd be in the drone unit, maybe leading it, and Sam would have time to move into something safer. The only worry is that money stays tight for a while with the car and the rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI every day and apply for the drone unit. I'd sell the car when the finance is half paid and start saving properly. Maybe I'd start a small side business teaching drone safety to farmers or estate agents, if the force approves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly, even a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a drone safety business look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weekend courses, maybe a hundred per person, teaching the rules and safe flying. There are farmers out past Hillcrest who use drones for crops and barely know the law. I'd need the force to sign off on it as secondary work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the robot date, 2039, worry you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. By 2039 I'd want to be in a role where I'm running machines, not competing with them. That's the whole plan, really.

say: This is the **best case**, with time to retrain people properly.
I'd say **start small** and learn the tools now.
think: Ten years puts me in the **drone unit**, maybe leading it.
Money stays **tight** for a while with the car and rent.
do: Keep using **AI daily** and apply for the drone unit.
Sell the car at **half paid** and start saving properly.
Start weekend **drone safety courses** if the force approves.
S4.quote: By 2039 I'd want to be in a role where I'm running machines, not competing with them.
fieldNote: With a decade, the **adaptive side** wins out over money worries.
His side business idea draws on **farmers near Hillcrest**.
Money remains **tight**, which keeps him short of fully calm.

steps.text: Keep using AI tools daily in patrol and study
Sell the car halfway through the finance and start saving
Run weekend drone safety courses for local farmers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Sam's job goes first and mine soon after, with no savings. What would help is funded retraining for partners like Sam, not just for officers, and some income support in the gap. Also a clear route for officers like me to supervise the new systems.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe about households. Everyone asks about jobs one at a time. In our house the question is what happens when one job goes and the other wobbles.
